title: Normalization 1NF to BCNF
summary: Removing insertion, update, and deletion anomalies step by step, from first normal form through Boyce-Codd normal form.

slides.markdown:
**Normalization** is the process of restructuring tables to eliminate redundancy-driven anomalies, guided by a sequence of increasingly strict rules called **normal forms** — 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, and beyond.

Each normal form fixes a specific class of problem the previous one leaves open. Skip straight to "just put everything in one table" and you get **anomalies**: the same fact stored in multiple places can drift out of sync, and you can't represent some facts at all without others being present.

This is the most heavily interview-tested topic in relational databases — expect to be handed a bad table and asked "what normal form is this, and how would you fix it?"

slides.sectionTitle: Insertion, update, and deletion anomalies (the why)
slides.markdown:
Consider one unnormalized table: `Enroll(student_id, student_name, course_id, course_title, instructor)`. Three anomalies fall out immediately. **Insertion anomaly**: you can't add a new course that has no students enrolled yet, because `student_id` is part of the key and can't be `NULL`. **Update anomaly**: if a course's `instructor` changes, you must update it in every row for every student enrolled in that course — miss one, and the data is now inconsistent with itself. **Deletion anomaly**: if the last student enrolled in a course drops it, deleting that row erases the only record that the course (`course_title`, `instructor`) ever existed.

All three anomalies have the same root cause: this one table is forcing together facts about *students*, facts about *courses*, and facts about *enrollment* that have independent lifecycles. Normalization is the mechanical process of splitting them back apart.

**1NF (First Normal Form)**: every attribute holds a single atomic value — no repeating groups, no comma-separated lists in one cell, no nested tables. A `phone_numbers` column holding `"555-1234, 555-5678"` violates 1NF.

**2NF**: the table is in 1NF, and every non-key attribute is **fully** functionally dependent on the *entire* primary key — no partial dependency on just part of a composite key (only relevant when the key is composite; every 1NF table with a single-column key is automatically in 2NF).

**3NF**: the table is in 2NF, and no non-key attribute is **transitively** dependent on the key — every non-key attribute must depend on the key directly, not depend on another non-key attribute that depends on the key. `course_id → instructor → office_number` chains a non-key attribute through another non-key attribute — a 3NF violation.

Each form is strictly stronger than the last — a table in 3NF is automatically in 2NF and 1NF.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a table decomposed through the normal forms
slides.markdown:
![Decomposing a table through 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF](assets/normalization-decomposition.svg)

Each panel removes exactly one class of anomaly: splitting off `phone_numbers` into its own table fixes the 1NF violation; splitting `Enroll` into `Students`, `Courses`, `Enrollments` fixes the partial dependency (2NF); splitting `instructor`'s own attributes (`office_number`) into a separate `Instructors` table fixes the transitive dependency (3NF).

Notice each step is driven by naming a specific functional dependency and asking "does this belong with the key, or with something else the key merely points at?"

**BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form)** tightens 3NF's rule: for every non-trivial FD `X → Y` in the table, X must be a **superkey** — full stop, with no exception for X being part of a candidate key (3NF has that exception; BCNF removes it).

The classic case where 3NF passes but BCNF fails: `Bookings(student_id, course_id, instructor)`, where each course has several possible instructors (so `{student_id, course_id}` is the key), but each instructor teaches only one course (`instructor → course_id`). `instructor` is not a superkey, yet it determines `course_id` — a real, non-trivial FD whose determinant isn't a superkey. This table is in 3NF (because `course_id` is part of the primary key, which is 3NF's carve-out) but violates BCNF.

BCNF is stricter and eliminates every redundancy 3NF theoretically still permits — but as the next slide shows, that strictness has a real cost.

| | 3NF | BCNF |
|---|---|---|
| Rule | Non-key attributes can't transitively depend on the key, with a carve-out when the determinant is part of a candidate key | Every determinant of a non-trivial FD must be a superkey — no carve-out |
| Redundancy eliminated | Most, but not all — the carve-out can still leave some | All — strictly less redundancy possible |
| Dependency preservation | Always achievable — you can always decompose to 3NF without losing the ability to check any original FD without a join | Not always achievable — some BCNF decompositions lose the ability to enforce an original FD without joining tables back together |
| Practical default | The common target for most schemas | Used when the extra redundancy elimination is worth losing dependency preservation |

**How to decide:** default to 3NF for most schemas — it removes the vast majority of real anomalies and always preserves dependency-checking. Reach for BCNF specifically when you've identified the exact 3NF carve-out case (a non-key determinant that's part of a candidate key) and the residual redundancy it allows is actually causing problems.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: lossy decomposition and the lossless-join test
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Any decomposition that removes a bad functional dependency is a safe normalization step."

**Why it's wrong:** a **lossy decomposition** splits a table into pieces that, when joined back together, produce *more* rows than the original — spurious tuples that never existed in the source data. This happens when the split columns don't include a common key that uniquely reconstructs the original rows. It's not merely inconvenient; it silently fabricates false facts that look like real data.

**Correct model:** apply the **lossless-join test**: a decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if and only if the common attributes (R1 ∩ R2) form a superkey of at least one of the two pieces. Every standard normalization algorithm (2NF, 3NF, BCNF synthesis) is specifically designed to guarantee this property automatically — but a decomposition invented ad hoc, without checking this condition, can easily fail it.

**4NF** addresses a different kind of redundancy that BCNF doesn't catch: a **multivalued dependency (MVD)**, written `X ↠ Y`, where X determines a *set* of independent Y values, unrelated to some other independent set Z also determined by X. Classic example: `Employee(emp_id, skill, language)` where an employee's skills and languages are completely independent of each other — every combination of that employee's skills × languages ends up needing a row, purely to satisfy the table shape, not because the combination itself means anything.

An employee with 3 skills and 2 languages needs 6 rows just to list all combinations, even though skills and languages have nothing to do with each other. 4NF fixes this by splitting into `Employee_Skills(emp_id, skill)` and `Employee_Languages(emp_id, language)` — two independent one-to-many relationships instead of one artificially combined many-to-many.

This is genuinely rare in practice compared to 1NF-3NF violations, but it's a real interview differentiator — most candidates stop at BCNF.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: normalizing a real table step by step
slides.markdown:
```text
Start: Invoice(invoice_id, customer_name, customer_email, product_id, product_name, qty, unit_price)

1NF check: every cell atomic -- OK, no repeating groups.

2NF check: key is (invoice_id, product_id).
  customer_name, customer_email depend only on invoice_id (partial) -> move out
  product_name, unit_price depend only on product_id (partial)      -> move out
  qty genuinely needs both invoice_id and product_id (full)         -> stays

Result:
  Invoices(invoice_id, customer_name, customer_email)
  Products(product_id, product_name, unit_price)
  Invoice_Items(invoice_id, product_id, qty)

3NF check on Invoices: does customer_email depend on customer_name (transitively) or on invoice_id directly?
  -> directly on invoice_id (each invoice's own snapshot) -- OK, already 3NF.
```

Notice the process is always the same: name the key, find every non-key attribute's *real* determinant, and split off anything that depends on less than the whole key or on another non-key attribute.

slides.sectionTitle: How far to normalize: the diminishing-returns question
slides.markdown:
3NF eliminates the overwhelming majority of real-world anomalies and is the de facto target for most OLTP schemas — it's the point where redundancy elimination stops paying for itself against the growing cost of extra joins. Pushing to BCNF, 4NF, or beyond is a deliberate choice for specific tables where you've identified concrete, ongoing redundancy the lower forms still allow — not a default target for the whole schema.

A staff-level answer to "should this table be in BCNF?" is never just "yes, more normal is always better" — it's "here's the specific redundancy 3NF still allows in this table, here's the anomaly it causes, and here's why the extra join cost is worth it here." The next topic (denormalization) covers the opposite pressure: deliberately reversing some of this for read performance once normalization has done its job.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: what an update anomaly actually costs
slides.markdown:
Concretely: an unnormalized `Enroll` table with 50,000 rows where a popular course has 2,000 enrolled students stores that course's `instructor` field redundantly 2,000 times. Change the instructor, and a correct update needs to touch all 2,000 rows atomically — miss the transaction boundary (a batch job that crashes halfway, or a script run twice with different logic) and you can end up with 2,000 rows split across two different "true" instructors, an inconsistency that has no automatic way to resolve itself.

After normalizing `instructor` into its own `Courses` row, the same change is a single-row `UPDATE` — no batching, no partial-failure risk, and no way for the data to become internally inconsistent, because there's now exactly one place the fact lives.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: normalizing without checking the lossless-join property
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I split `Bookings(guest_name, room_number, room_type)` into `T1(guest_name, room_type)` and `T2(room_number, room_type)` because that removes the FD I was worried about, so it must be a valid decomposition."

**Why it's wrong:** the common attribute here is `room_type`, and unless `room_type` is a superkey of at least one of the two pieces (it usually isn't — many rooms share a type, and many guests could theoretically book the same type), joining `T1` and `T2` back together on `room_type` can produce spurious combinations of guests and rooms that were never actually booked together. The decomposition is lossy even though it looks reasonable at a glance.

**Correct model:** always verify the common attributes form a superkey of one side before trusting a decomposition — don't decompose purely by "does this remove the bad FD," because a decomposition can fix one problem (a functional dependency violation) while introducing a worse one (fabricated rows on join). Real normalization algorithms build in this check; ad hoc decompositions frequently skip it.

slides.sectionTitle: In an interview: naming the normal form of a table
slides.markdown:
When handed a table and asked "what normal form is this in, and why isn't it in the next one," the fast, structured approach is: check 1NF first (any repeating groups or non-atomic cells?), then check whether the key is composite (if not, 2NF is automatic — jump straight to 3NF), then look for any non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute (transitive dependency, a 3NF violation), then finally check whether every determinant of every non-trivial FD is a superkey (BCNF).

The strongest interview answers name the *specific* functional dependency causing the violation ("instructor determines office_number, and instructor isn't a key — that's the transitive dependency breaking 3NF") rather than a vague "this table has some redundancy." That precision is what separates "I've memorized the definitions" from "I can actually apply them."
